ideas.title: The Ringers of Saxby Green
ideas.short_description: In 1820 the church bells are the village's voice. Captain eight ringers on eight ropes, call the changes for weddings, funerals and fairs, and ring a three-hour peal without a slip.
ideas.description: In a Suffolk parish in 1820, the church bells announce every christening, wedding, funeral, harvest home and piece of news from London, and the ringers who pull them are the proudest folk in the village. You are their new captain, and the rival band from the market town across the river has never let you forget it. Eight bells hang in the tower, each heavy as a cart horse and swung full circle on a rope. They sound one after another in rounds, and you call out which neighbouring pair should swap places next, so the order wanders through thousands of rows without repeating. Moment to moment you pull your own rope in steady time, call the changes, and listen for the ringer who has drifted late or lost their place. Between practices you recruit the blacksmith, the schoolmistress, the poacher and the miller's daughter, teach them to handle a rope without being hauled off their feet, settle quarrels over the beer money, and keep the peace with a curate who thinks it all far too loud. The goal is a full peal, five thousand changes without a fault, for the squire's wedding.
ideas.pitch: English change ringing becomes the game: you lead a village band of bell ringers, calling the swaps in a pattern that must never repeat while keeping eight amateur villagers in time.

ideas.title: Dawn Caller
ideas.short_description: Cairo, 1935. Through the thirty nights of Ramadan, walk the old city's alleys with a small drum before dawn and call every family by name, so no one sleeps through the last meal before the fast.
ideas.description: In the old quarter of Cairo in 1935, the nights of Ramadan belong to the dawn caller: the person who walks the alleys in the dark hours with a small drum and a lantern, stopping at each door to call the family by name and wake them for the meal before the day's fast begins. Your father did it for forty years; this year it is your turn. Each evening you plan your route through a maze of lanes, courtyards and stairways, because every household must be woken in time to cook and eat before the call to prayer. Moment to moment you walk, beat a steady rhythm, and sing short rhymed greetings for each door, using the right names and a kind word for the sick widow or the new baby. Children follow you, shopkeepers offer tea, and grumpy neighbours shout from balconies. Forget a family and they will not forgive you. At the end of the month, the people you woke repay you with sweets, coins and cloth for the feast. The goal is to earn the trust of the whole quarter.
ideas.pitch: A route-planning and drumming game about the Ramadan dawn caller: across thirty nights you wake every household in an old Cairo quarter by name, in time, before the fast begins.

ideas.title: Forty Thousand Words
ideas.short_description: London, 1747. A group of booksellers has paid you to write the first great English dictionary in three years. Hire copyists, mark up every book you own and define forty thousand words before the money runs out.
ideas.description: In 1747 a group of London booksellers pays you a large advance to do what no one has done: write a complete dictionary of English, with a quotation from a great writer for every meaning of every word, in three years. You rent a garret off Fleet Street, hire six copyists, some of them drunk, and fill the room with borrowed books. Moment to moment you read through poets, sermons, law books and gardening manuals, mark the sentences that show a word's meaning, and pass them to your copyists to cut into slips. Then, word by word, you sort the slips, decide how many meanings each word has, write a definition for each and choose the best quotation. Some definitions are a joy; others take a week. Lenders want their books back with your pencil marks rubbed out, creditors knock at the door, and a lord who once ignored you suddenly wants credit. The booksellers want pages, not perfection. The goal is to finish before the advance is gone and the rival French academy can laugh.
ideas.pitch: You write an 18th-century dictionary against a deadline: gather quotations, split each word into its meanings and pick the best example, while managing copyists, creditors and the money left.

ideas.title: Saturday Night Noisemaker
ideas.short_description: In 1925 the pictures are silent, but the miners in the hall still hear every gunshot, train whistle and custard pie. Stand behind the screen with your box of noisemakers and play the film live.
ideas.description: In 1925 films have no soundtrack, so the miners' hall in a Welsh valley town hires someone to stand behind the screen on Saturday nights and make the noises live. That someone is you, a pit boy with quick hands. Your kit is a bass drum, a bicycle bell, a train whistle, coconut shells, a crank wind machine, a cap pistol, a sheet of tin and a bucket of coal, and the chapel organist at the piano will not wait for you. Moment to moment you watch the film flicker through the back of the screen, mirrored and blurry, and hit each noise as it happens: a door slam, a car horn, a cowboy's six-gun, a custard pie in the face. Miss the moment and the whole hall laughs at you instead of the picture; get the slapstick timing right and the benches shake. Between shows you work your shift underground, build new noisemakers, and argue with the projectionist about which reels to rent. The goal is to keep the hall full through a long strike.
ideas.pitch: A prop-based timing game in which you perform the sound effects for silent films live from behind the screen, picking the right noisemaker and hitting each on-screen moment for a mining-town crowd.

ideas.title: The Prompter's Trapdoor
ideas.short_description: Bombay, 1890. Hide beneath the stage of a touring theatre company and whisper forgotten lines to its stars, through songs, sword fights and painted thunderstorms.
ideas.description: In 1890 a theatre company from Bombay tours the railway towns of India, performing grand dramas full of songs, magic, sword fights and painted thunderstorms, in three languages on three different nights. The stars are famous, the plays are long, and nobody knows every line. That is why the company keeps you, the prompter, crouched beneath a trapdoor at the front of the stage with the only complete script and an oil lamp. Moment to moment you follow the play line by line, watch the actors' faces for the frozen look of a forgotten speech or verse, and whisper the next words at the right moment and volume. Too early and you insult the proud leading man; too loud and the front rows laugh; too late and the demon king stands silent while the princess waits to be rescued. Actors skip scenes, add songs the crowd demands and switch languages mid-act, and you must find your place again fast. Between shows the company travels by train, and you learn each actor's habits and settle backstage feuds. The goal is to bring the company home from its longest tour.
ideas.pitch: You play the hidden prompter of a touring theatre company, saving live shows by whispering the right line at the right moment and volume while the actors improvise, skip scenes and switch languages.

ideas.title: Three Miles in the Dark
ideas.short_description: Yorkshire, 1830. The canal tunnel is three miles long, pitch dark and has no towpath, so you lie on a plank across the boat and walk it through with your boots on the dripping walls.
ideas.description: In 1830 the canal crosses the Pennine hills through a tunnel three miles long, too narrow for a towpath, so the horses are led over the moor while the boats are pushed through by men lying on their backs. You are one of those men, a legger, paid a shilling a trip from a hut at the tunnel mouth. You and your partner lie on planks laid across the boat's bow, and by the light of a single candle you walk the boat along by pressing your boots against the wet walls, step by step, in steady rhythm. Moment to moment you keep time with your partner, shorten your stride where the tunnel narrows, call out at passing places, and save your strength for the long stretch where water pours from the roof and the air turns foul. Push out of step and the boat scrapes and stalls; go too fast and your legs give out halfway. Between trips you bargain with boat families, drink at the tunnel inn, nurse your knees and train new partners. Play alone or with a friend on the second plank, and become the fastest pair on the canal before the railway arrives.
ideas.pitch: A two-person rhythm and stamina game about 'legging', where you lie on your back and walk a canal boat through a dark three-mile tunnel by pushing your feet against the walls in step with a partner.

ideas.title: The Drum That Speaks
ideas.short_description: West Africa, 1850. The language here rises and falls in pitch, and so does your drum. Listen to the next town's drummer across the forest, work out the words, and beat the message on toward the palace.
ideas.description: In the Yoruba towns of 1850, speech is musical: every word rises and falls in pitch, and a skilled drummer can make a talking drum say almost anything by squeezing its cords to bend the note. You are the new royal drummer of a small town on the road between the coast and a king's palace, and you are still learning the drum's language. Moment to moment you listen to the next town's drumming drift across the forest, write down its high, middle and low beats, and work out which words and proverbs they could stand for, since many words share the same melody and only context tells them apart. Then you drum the message onward, squeezing and striking in the right pattern so the town beyond can understand it. Messages announce births, deaths, markets, visiting traders and approaching danger, and one wrong word turns a wedding into a funeral. At court you drum praise names for chiefs and guests, where a clever proverb wins favour. Between messages you carve drums, train apprentices and learn the history of every family. The goal is to become the drummer whose word the king trusts.
ideas.pitch: A decoding and relay puzzle built on the Yoruba talking drum: you work out tonal drum messages from the next town by context and pass them on accurately, where one wrong word changes the news.

ideas.title: Bellfast Tower
ideas.short_description: 1919. The bells of St Anne's fell silent when the village ringers went to war and never came home. Rehang the bells, recruit a band of complete beginners, and teach them to ring before the new year.
ideas.description: Bellfast Tower begins in an English village church a year after the Great War. The old band of ringers marched away in 1914 and none of them returned, and the bells have hung silent ever since. The ropes are rotten, a bell is cracked and nobody remembers how it was done. With the vicar's blessing and a handful of volunteers, you set out to bring them back. Ringing is hard physical work: each bell weighs as much as a small car and swings a full circle with every pull, and the band must keep perfect time as the bells swap places in long patterns called methods. Teach a farmer, a schoolgirl, a shy postman and a wounded soldier to handle a rope safely, then to ring rounds, then to ring changes. Mend the frame, raise money at the fete and keep the band together through grief and harvests. Play alone with computer ringers or with friends online, each holding one rope, and ring the village into the new year.
ideas.pitch: A co-op rhythm game built on English church change-ringing, where each player handles one physically swinging bell and the band must ring permutation patterns together without a clash.

ideas.title: Seating Europe
ideas.short_description: Vienna, 1905. As head waiter of Europe's grandest hotel dining room, seat diplomats, bankers and countesses so that the right people meet, the wrong ones never do, and every dinner ends in toasts.
ideas.description: In 1905 the dining room of a grand Vienna hotel is where the fate of Europe is quietly arranged between the soup and the coffee, and you are its head waiter. Every evening ambassadors, archdukes, bankers, composers, cavalry officers and countesses reserve tables, and you decide where each one sits, who faces whom and who can overhear which conversation. Each guest has a rank, a temper, a secret and a list of people they cannot stand. Moment to moment you place name cards on a floor plan of tables, read notes from the doorman and the cloakroom girl, and redraw the plan when a late telegram arrives or a duchess appears without a booking. Then the evening unfolds: a quiet table by the palms may let a treaty be agreed, while an insult across the room ends in pistols at dawn. Meanwhile a polite gentleman from the police pays you to seat certain guests where he can listen, and you must decide whose side you are on. The goal is to keep the peace of Europe for one more season.
ideas.pitch: A seating-chart logic puzzle used as quiet diplomacy: where you seat each guest, and who can overhear whom, decides treaties, duels and police informing in a 1905 hotel dining room.

ideas.title: Landfall Captions
ideas.short_description: Work the overnight shift as the live captioner at a small-town TV station. Type every word spoken on air in real time while a hurricane cuts the town off, and your captions become its lifeline.
ideas.description: Landfall Captions puts you in a cramped booth at a local television station on the night a hurricane makes landfall. You are the live captioner: everything said on air must appear as text within seconds, so viewers who cannot hear the broadcast know where to go and when to leave. Anchors improvise, reporters shout over the wind, and the emergency office reads out road closures and shelter addresses that must be typed exactly right. A wrong street name can send people the wrong way. When the power goes and the station switches to radio, your captions on the website become the only place deaf viewers can follow the news. Between broadcasts the phone rings with questions, the station manager pushes for ratings, and the building leaks. You decide what to keep when the anchor speaks faster than anyone can type, and whether to post a warning nobody approved. Six real-time hours of rising water, and every word counts.
ideas.pitch: A real-time typing game where you are a TV station's live captioner during a hurricane, and your speed, accuracy and choices about what to keep decide which deaf viewers reach safety.

ideas.title: Coconuts and Thunder
ideas.short_description: It is 1938 and the radio play goes out live in ten minutes. You make every sound the listeners hear, from horses and storms to gunshots and slammed doors, with nothing but a table full of junk.
ideas.description: Coconuts and Thunder puts you at the sound effects table of a radio drama studio in the golden age of broadcasting. Actors read the script into the microphone and you make the world around them, live, with no second take. Coconut shells become galloping horses, crumpled cellophane becomes a crackling fire, a box of gravel becomes footsteps, and a sheet of tin becomes thunder. Follow the script, watch the director's hand signals, and hit every cue at exactly the right moment. A late door slam ruins a murder scene. A wrong sound turns a love story into a comedy. Between shows you build new props from whatever you can find, invent sounds for scripts that ask for impossible things like a rocket landing on the moon, and keep up with a cast that loves to improvise. Play alone or with friends on the same couch, each running part of the table, and keep the nation listening every week.
ideas.pitch: You are the live sound-effects artist on a 1930s radio drama, hitting script cues with household props in real time and building new props between broadcasts.

ideas.title: Heave and Sing
ideas.short_description: Lead the work songs on a tea clipper racing from China to London in 1866. Every rope is hauled by hand, and the crew pull only as fast and as long as you can keep them singing.
ideas.description: Heave and Sing puts you aboard a sleek tea clipper in the great race to bring the season's first tea from China to London, ninety-nine days across three oceans. You are the shantyman, the sailor whose job is to sing. Raising the anchor, setting sail and pumping the hold are all done by hand, and a crew only pulls together when someone keeps the rhythm. Choose the right song for each job, call the verses, and hold the beat so thirty sailors haul at the same moment. Sing too fast and they tire. Sing too slow and the sail is not set before the squall hits, and the rival ships pull ahead. Between watches you learn songs from sailors of a dozen countries, make up verses about the cook, and lift the spirits of a crew that shares no single language. Play alone or with friends online, each hauling a line, and bring your ship into London first.
ideas.pitch: A rhythm game turned into an ocean race: as the ship's shantyman you set the tempo of the crew's work, and your ship's speed against rival clippers depends on how well you keep the beat.

ideas.title: Saddlebag Nurse
ideas.short_description: Kentucky mountains, 1925. You are a nurse-midwife on horseback, the only care for hundreds of families spread across hollows with no roads. Ride out in any weather and bring mothers and babies through.
ideas.description: Saddlebag Nurse follows a young nurse-midwife on her first posting to a remote mountain district where the nearest hospital is two days away. Her clinic is a log cabin, her ambulance is a horse called Pepper, and her patients live up creeks and ridges that no car can reach. Each day you plan rounds across the district map, fording rivers, climbing trails and checking on expecting mothers, sick children and old folks living alone. Then a rider arrives at night, and you set out to a birth in the rain. At the bedside you work with what is in your saddlebags: listen, feel the baby's position, time the labour and watch for the warning signs that mean you must act. Families are proud, suspicious of outsiders and full of their own remedies, and trust is earned one visit at a time. Care for your horse, keep careful records, and get the whole district through a year of floods, fevers and snow.
ideas.pitch: A medical game played on horseback: you plan rounds across a roadless 1920s mountain district as a nurse-midwife, then handle births at the bedside with only what fits in your saddlebags.

ideas.title: Doorstep 1917
ideas.short_description: It is 1917 and the boys have gone to war, so the post office hires you. Ride your bicycle through town with telegrams of births, business and death, and learn to read a face before you hand one over.
ideas.description: Doorstep 1917 is a story about the young people who carried news through a small industrial town during the First World War. Every morning you collect envelopes at the post office counter and ride out through cobbled streets, steep hills and factory yards. Some telegrams are good news: a wedding, a birth, an order for the mill. Some are the ones every family dreads, from the War Office, and people learn to fear the sight of your cap. Plan your route, beat the clock for urgent messages, and decide how to deliver the hardest ones: wait with a mother until a neighbour comes, find the father at the factory first, or hand it over and ride on. Your bicycle needs repairs, your wages help feed your family, and the older messengers think a girl will not last a month. Over a year you come to know every street and every family. Finish the year with your job, your conscience and your friends.
ideas.pitch: A bicycle delivery game where the hard part comes after you arrive: as a wartime telegram messenger you decide how to break good and terrible news to the same families all year.

ideas.title: Sky Post of Paris
ideas.short_description: Paris, 1870. The city is under siege and the only way out is up. Launch mail balloons by night, and bring replies home on pigeons carrying thousands of letters shrunk onto a film no bigger than a thumbnail.
ideas.description: Sky Post of Paris is set during the four-month siege of Paris. Enemy armies surround the city and every road is cut. You run the post that keeps it talking to the world. Turn empty railway stations into workshops where seamstresses stitch and varnish cotton balloons, fill them from the city gas mains, and train navy sailors to fly them. Each night you read the wind and decide whether to launch. Once aloft, a balloon cannot be steered, so you guide it only by dropping sand to climb or venting gas to sink into a better wind, and a bad choice carries it into enemy hands. Outgoing balloons carry letters and baskets of homing pigeons. The replies come back on those pigeons, thousands of messages photographed onto tiny films tucked into a feather quill. When a bird lands in your loft, project the film onto a wall and have clerks copy every message by hand. Manage cloth, gas, crews and hope until the siege ends.
ideas.pitch: A two-way logistics game set in the 1870 siege of Paris: balloons you cannot steer carry the mail out, and homing pigeons carrying microfilm letters bring the replies back.

ideas.title: The Airlock Kitchen
ideas.short_description: Six divers will live inside a sealed pressure chamber for twenty-eight days while they repair a pipeline on the seabed. You are the ship's cook, and every one of their meals goes in through a tiny airlock.
ideas.description: The Airlock Kitchen is set on a diving support ship working in the North Sea. Six saturation divers live sealed inside a steel chamber on deck, kept at the pressure of the seabed, and each day a bell lowers them to repair a broken pipeline a hundred metres below. They cannot come out for a month. You are the ship's cook. You feed forty sailors in the mess and pass the divers' meals through a small airlock in the chamber wall. Under pressure, bread collapses, flavours fade and the helium in the air makes the divers cold and hungry all the time. Plan menus that keep them warm and strong, time meals around dives and rest, and follow their work on the seabed through the helmet cameras in the dive control room, where a tired, hungry diver starts making mistakes. Storms toss the galley and the supply boat runs late. Keep the whole ship fed and bring every diver home.
ideas.pitch: A cooking and management game where you feed saturation divers sealed in a pressure chamber for a month, and how well you feed them shows up in their work on the seabed.

ideas.title: Unauthorised Carols
ideas.short_description: A censorship simulator with a guitar. Christmas has been banned in a post-war country, but your rock band is touring anyway. Edit your lyrics past the censors, play each gig in rhythm and shape the people's opinion one carol at a time.
ideas.description:
In a grey post-war country governed by the recently elected Loyalist Party, carols are now classified as unauthorised gatherings. As the songwriter of the Sleigh Bells, the last independent rock band in the country, your job is to get the music through.

Before every concert the setlist goes to the local censor's office. Read the new regulations, remove and edit words, swap whole verses and decide which songs to hide inside harmless folk tunes. Every edit changes the people's opinion, the band's reputation and the interest of the secret police.

Then the curtain rises. Play rock versions of famous Christmas songs in a simple rhythm game, and choose in the moment whether to sing the approved lyric or the real one. The crowd reacts to every choice, and so do the officers in the back row.

Between towns, read letters from fans, smugglers and tired bureaucrats. Bring the holiday back to a frightened country, or play it safe and keep the band together until Christmas Eve.
ideas.pitch: A censorship sim where the text you edit is your own band's Christmas rock lyrics, and the rhythm game is where you decide in real time whether to sing the approved line or the forbidden one.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are The Westport Independent (editing a newspaper under a dystopian party, shaping public opinion) and Santa Rockstar (casual Christmas rock rhythm game). The decoded tags lead with Simulation, Choices Matter, Story Rich, Casual and Text-Based. Putting the lyric-censorship simulation first and the rhythm gigs second landed closest. A radio-censor version and a North Pole newspaper version both scored lower.

ideas.title: Seating Plan: 1943
ideas.short_description: A cozy strategy-flavoured logic puzzle set during the 1943 North Africa campaign of World War II. As protocol officer of a secret Allied summit, find the perfect seat for hilariously particular generals, diplomats and staff, each with pet peeves, without starting a second war at dinner.
ideas.description:
North Africa, January 1943. While tank columns fight across the desert, the Allied leaders gather at a seaside hotel to plan the next stage of World War II, and somebody has to decide where everyone sits. That somebody is you.

Every level is a seating puzzle drawn from the summit's busy days: the opening banquet, a cramped briefing room, the motorcade to the airfield, a press photograph on the hotel steps. Each guest has a portrait card listing what they need and what they cannot stand. The admiral must face the sea, the general refuses to sit below the air marshal, two interpreters must stay beside their delegations and the war correspondent cannot be within earshot of anything secret.

Drag guests into place, watch their moods change and rearrange until the whole table is satisfied. New rules arrive as the summit goes on, from blackout curtains to surprise guests. Between puzzles, short historical notes explain the real conference behind the comedy. It is a light, top-down logic game about the small human details behind the big decisions of the war.
ideas.pitch: A cozy seating-arrangement logic puzzle set at a 1943 North African Allied summit, where the strategy of the war comes down to who refuses to sit next to whom.
ideas.interpretation: This fuses a cozy logic game about seating people with pet peeves with a WWII North Africa 1943 strategy sim. The decoded tags (Puzzle, Casual, Logic, Strategy, WWII, Historical, Top-Down) suggested a non-violent historical logic game. The summit protocol-officer framing beat both a quartermaster seating version and a unit-deployment puzzle wargame.

ideas.title: Contraband Beard
ideas.short_description: Your beard grows while you sleep. Birds nest in it. It remembers everything. And in this kingdom, beards are illegal.
ideas.description: Grow the longest beard in the land, in a kingdom where beards are against the law. Royal barbers patrol every road, and a bare chin is the only safe chin. You are an old man whose beard has a mind of its own. Every night you sleep it grows a little longer, and it seems to be alive: sparrows nest in it, it stirs when danger is near, and it remembers the places it has brushed against. By day you wander villages, forests and castle towns, ducking into haystacks whenever a barber passes; by night you find somewhere safe to sleep. You explore, you hide, you sleep, and the beard grows. A longer beard is harder to hide, but it can lift, catch and remember things a shaven chin never could. Online, players can take the role of royal barbers and hunt each other's beards across the same countryside. Play it alone as a gentle, strange story about growing old in a kingdom that has forgotten its grandfathers, or online as a game of hide and seek.
ideas.pitch: A third-person stealth and exploration sim where your growing, living beard is your progression, your tool and the contraband you must hide, with an optional online mode where players act as royal barbers hunting it.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags call for a 3D third-person atmospheric exploration sim with a minor PvP strand. The odd parents and neighbours (mustache games, a masseuse sim, a tiny hero exploring a house) shared a theme of whimsical body care. Probing showed beard and barber premises scoring far above everything else, and adding the outlawed-beard and hide-from-barbers stealth twist gave the jump from 0.37 to 0.46.

ideas.title: Seeds of Freedom
ideas.short_description: A third-person adventure about football, board games and history in a West African village.
ideas.description: It is early 1957 and Kofi has come home from the city to his grandfather's village on the Gold Coast, weeks before the country becomes Ghana. The village football club has been invited to play an exhibition match on Independence Day, and Kofi wants a place on the team. In this relaxed third-person 3D adventure you wander the market, the cocoa farms, the mission school and the chief's courtyard, talking to neighbours, running errands and training on the red dirt pitch by the river. Football matches are quick, arcade-style kickabouts that anyone can play. In the evenings the elders gather to play Oware, and beating them at the ancient board game is the only way to earn their stories about the cocoa boom, the colonial schools and the long road to freedom. A short, gentle and educational adventure about a real moment in history, told through sport, games and the people who played them.
ideas.pitch: An educational third-person village adventure set on the eve of Ghana's independence, where you earn your place through street football and Oware matches, and winning at the board game unlocks oral history.
ideas.interpretation: The neighbours are small regional-culture games (dominoes, a Brazilian city tour, a Polish commune, an African-president sim), and the decoded tags add adventure, historical, sports, board game, education and walking sim. The hole reads as a culturally specific historical walking adventure built around a traditional board game and sport. A Ghana 1957 setting beat Korean, Brazilian and Irish versions by a wide margin.

ideas.title: The Ashcombe Idol
ideas.short_description: Hired as consultant on a maverick director's new film about an ancient cult, a history professor finds the prop idol on set is real. Unlock its secrets in 3D match-3 action puzzles and find out whether you are filming a story or starring in one.
ideas.description:
Professor Tom Avery was hired to make a maverick director's period film look historically accurate. Then the crew moves into the real Ashcombe University, the director unveils an idol borrowed from the college museum, and the actors start forgetting their lines in favour of words none of them should know.

Explore the campus and the half-built film sets in third person, reading old expedition journals, script rewrites and letters from the museum's founders. When the idol stirs, the game becomes an action puzzle: a rotating 3D lattice of carved stones where you swap neighbours to line up three or more matching symbols, setting off chain reactions before the lattice seals itself again.

Each solved lattice unlocks new rooms, new footage and new truths. The faster you clear it, the more the director films, and the more the idol seems to be watching back.

Has Tom become the unwitting star of the film, or has he stumbled into something far older than history?
ideas.pitch: A story-driven mystery on a film set where every sealed secret is a rotating 3D match-3 lattice, so the investigation moves forward through puzzle chains instead of dialogue trees.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are Old Gods Rising (a professor consulting on a strange film at a university, a cosmic mystery) and Critical Mass (3D action match-3). The decoded tags are mostly Puzzle, plus Story Rich, Strategy, Historical and Realistic. Leaning on horror wording pulled the draft toward horror games, so the best version keeps a 'period film' and 'historical idol' framing and makes the 3D match-3 the way into the mystery.

ideas.title: Black Door Holdings
ideas.short_description: When his wealthiest patient vanishes, a Victorian psychiatrist is left in charge of the man's oil enterprise. Grow the business of black gold from a few wells into a global empire, while the search drags you deeper into a conspiracy of darkness and madness.
ideas.description:
England, 1891. Dr. Edmund Hale's most troubled patient, the oil baron Silas Crane, disappears the night after describing a black door at the bottom of his deepest well. His will names Hale as the trustee of everything he owns.

By day you run the oil enterprise: buy new fields, hire crews and engineers, sign contracts with railway barons, invest in refineries and ride the rise and fall of crude prices to keep the shareholders loyal. By night you search for your patient in pixel-art point-and-click scenes, questioning frightened workers, reading his session notes and examining strange core samples brought up from below.

Profit and dread are bound together. The richest wells reach the deepest places, and every barrel sold buys a little more knowledge and a little less sanity. Choose which fields to open and which to seal, whom to pay and whom to silence.

Rise from reluctant trustee to oil magnate, or follow Crane into the madness waiting beneath his empire. Several endings await.
ideas.pitch: An oil-tycoon management sim and a Lovecraftian point-and-click mystery are one loop: the psychiatrist hunting his missing patient has to run the patient's oil empire, and every profitable well drills closer to the horror.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are The Last Door S2 (a psychiatrist searching for a missing client, Victorian pixel-art horror) and Oil Enterprise (growing from one oilfield to an oil magnate). The decoded tags put Management, Economy and Story Rich on top, so I made the psychiatrist the trustee of his patient's oil company. My first draft, an inherited 1920s company, scored lower (0.38), and an asylum-business version drifted toward sanatorium sims.

ideas.title: Bitter Remedies
ideas.short_description: Become a self-taught back-alley chemist in 1888 London and discover the darker side of chemistry. Mix dubious concoctions for strange customers, then help hunt the killer stalking the fog before your own bottles convict you.
ideas.description:
Whitechapel, autumn 1888. Your little back-alley shop sells hair tonics, miracle lotions and the occasional black-market mixture that is better not asked about. Business is fine until a bottle with your label is found beside a victim of the most feared killer in England, and a sharp-eyed detective starts dropping by every evening with polite questions.

Days are spent behind the counter. Brewing is simple, just tip one flask into another and see what happens, but every customer wants something different and you decide what you are willing to make and who you will sell it to. Watch your stock, money and reputation, because every bottle may come back as evidence.

Nights belong to the investigation. Run real Victorian chemistry tests on the samples the detective leaves with you, match handwriting in your order book and point and click through foggy streets to question regulars and suspects. Each clue can clear your name or tighten the noose, depending on what you choose to reveal. Darkly funny, gently paced and full of moral choices, it is a detective story told from the wrong side of the counter.
ideas.pitch: A Victorian murder mystery told from behind the counter of a shady chemist's shop: the bottles you sell by day are the evidence you must analyse by night, and they may convict you.
ideas.interpretation: This fuses a darkly comic black-market concoction-mixing sim with a Victorian Whitechapel detective adventure. The decoded tags (Casual, Simulation, Detective, Management, Choices Matter, Point & Click) fit a shop-management loop that feeds an investigation. Making the chemist both supplier and suspect scored best.

ideas.title: Good Dog, Old Games
ideas.short_description: School trips are tough for an eight-year-old who is blind, and tougher when the class leaves him locked inside a video game museum after dark. You play as his lifelong canine companion: guide him through fifty years of playable history and help him escape.
ideas.description:
First days at school are tough enough. Ollie's first class trip is to the national museum of video games, and he cannot see a single screen. He has Juno, his guide dog, and a head full of old games his dad taught him to play by sound. When the class leaves without them and the lights go out, the two of them are on their own.

You play as Juno. Every gallery is a different decade, and every exhibit still runs: dozens of playable classics, from 1970s paddle games to 1980s arcade cabinets and 1990s home consoles. Ollie holds your harness while you lead him through side-scrolling rooms, sniff out safe paths, push switches, bark warnings and work out which old machines open which doors.

Along the way, recorded interviews with designers, original sketches and design documents in each gallery tell the story of how games were made, and hide the clues you need to get out. A gentle, old-school adventure about trust, history and seeing the world differently.
ideas.pitch: An escort-puzzle adventure where a guide dog leads a blind boy through a museum of video game history after dark, and the playable retro exhibits are the locks on every door.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are a guide-dog escort adventure (a dog protecting a blind boy at school) and an interactive documentary anthology of 50 years of games. The decoded tags (Retro, 1980s/1990s, Historical, Family Friendly, Side Scroller) suggested a gentle, history-filled escort adventure. A text-adventure reading scored lower.

ideas.title: Wallcode 1920
ideas.short_description: In a frontier town in 1920, orders are written on walls. Paint codes for your squad, break the enemy's, and reach every checkpoint first.
ideas.description:
Wallcode 1920 is a realistic first-person war game where two teams paint the walls, break each other's codes and race to the checkpoints. Neither army trusts the radio, so orders are left in paint and chalk.

Every street is an arena. You carry a paint pot, a stick of chalk and a cipher notebook. Paint a symbol and your squad obeys it: wait, cross, breach. Enemy scouts paint their own, so you copy their marks, break the cipher in your notebook and paint over them to send their runners into a dead end. Hold every checkpoint before they do and the district is yours.

Between missions the story plays out as an illustrated visual novel in the signals office, where officers, couriers and a suspected traitor test your loyalty. Every run builds a new town with fresh ciphers; fall, and you begin again with what you learned and a new class unlocked: the runner, the codebreaker or the forger who can copy enemy handwriting.
ideas.pitch: A first-person war fought only through painted wall-codes: you guide your squad with symbols, crack and over-paint the enemy's chalk ciphers, and race their runners through the streets, with the story told as a visual novel between roguelite runs.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags are weak and scattered (first-person, strategy, realistic, visual novel, 2D/3D). The parents mix a 1920 war cipher game, a paint-the-map party game, a checkpoint-racing arena and a phone-operator visual novel. Probing showed the direction rewards genre mixes and penalises cozy or animal themes, so I combined cipher-breaking, wall-painting, checkpoint races and visual-novel interludes into one 1920 game.

ideas.title: Prime Time Planet
ideas.short_description: A pixel-art game show adventure about one stubborn mechanic trying to win back her family's farm on live television.
ideas.description: Welcome to Prime Time Planet, the most watched game show on television. Rook, a stubborn mechanic from a mining colony, signs up to win back her family's farm, and you guide her through every episode. On stage, every challenge is a small test of timing and nerve: cross collapsing bridges, dodge spotlights and answer the host's riddles before the buzzer. Between rounds you switch to the control room, a casual strategy screen where ratings become currency: buy sponsor gear, bribe the set designers, choose which hazards to face next and which rival contestants to sabotage. Backstage, you point and click through dressing rooms, prop stores and the editing suite to find tools, allies and secrets. The show is difficult and the hosts are cruel, yet the season follows a linear story with a beginning, a twist and a finale. Every episode Rook survives adds a little more to her kit and her fan club, so a run that starts fragile ends with a contestant the whole planet roots for. Can she survive twelve episodes, win the audience, save the farm and expose the network behind the cameras?
ideas.pitch: A linear, story-driven pixel adventure in which you are both the contestant on a cruel TV game show and her backstage schemer, spending ratings on sponsors and sabotage between short skill rounds.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags (2D pixel, casual, adventure, strategy, point & click, story rich, linear, female protagonist, incremental, difficult) and the heaviest parent (Pixel Gladiator's televised survival show) pointed to a broadcast-contest frame. Library, food-stall and photo-mystery takes scored far lower. The TV-show framing with a heroine and a strategy layer between stages was the only one that climbed.

ideas.title: Nora Off the Page
ideas.short_description: Run through the pages of a talking pop-up book. Each chapter is read aloud and fully animated, then turns into a fast, cute runner as Nora races to catch the little aliens escaping from her bedtime story.
ideas.description: Nora Off the Page is a colorful story adventure for families. Nora's favorite pop-up book is about a crew of tiny aliens, and tonight they have decided to leave it. With every alien that escapes, the story falls apart. Each chapter starts like a voiced storybook, with animated 3D pages, words that light up as they are read and simple choices about what Nora says and where she looks next. Then the chase begins and the game becomes a bright arcade runner. Sprint across paper meadows, cardboard rooftops and the inside of a birthday cake, jump over puddles of spilled ink, slide under fences and collect stars while the runaway aliens zip ahead in their tiny saucers. Catch them and they return to the page, adding new scenes, songs and jokes to the story. Chapters are short and linear, controls are just jump and slide, and a gentle mode keeps younger players going. Funny, warm and quick, it is a story you can read and run.
ideas.pitch: A voiced, read-along pop-up storybook where each chapter turns into a cute arcade runner, chasing the runaway aliens back onto the page to rebuild the story.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are roughly equal shares of a children's read-along storybook visual novel (Maggie's Farmyard Adventure), an arcade shooter (MINUS ZERO) and a cute female-led alien-food runner (Galactic Gluttony). I joined them as a voiced storybook visual novel with runner chapters about escaping aliens, and kept away from Galactic Gluttony's agent-eats-food premise.

ideas.title: Billy-Jo and the Martian Gallery
ideas.short_description: A kid genius, a homemade rocket and an alien art gallery haunted by ghost dogs: a cute little 1990s-style horror adventure. Explore the dark halls, find the keys, admire the artwork and get back to Earth before bedtime without getting licked.
ideas.description:
Billy-Jo is eight, a certified backyard genius, and slightly lost. His homemade rocket ship has run out of fuel on Mars, and the only building for miles is a grand gallery of Martian art, closed for the night and full of ghosts. Friendly ones. Mostly. They are dogs, and they want to lick you.

Point, click and sneak through the gallery's echoing wings in chunky 1990s pixel art. Each room hides a puzzle built from its paintings and sculptures: line up a cosmic portrait, rotate a statue, decode the brushstrokes to find the keys that unlock the next hall and the fuel cells for your rocket. Ghost pups drift between the exhibits, sniffing for you; hide behind plinths, toss a squeaky toy to distract them or zap them with your trusty toy ray gun to buy a few seconds.

Spooky but never cruel, short and replayable, it is a love letter to the shareware adventures of the early nineties, with a gallery full of dogs that just want a friend.
ideas.pitch: An early-90s shareware-style sci-fi adventure in which a backyard rocket kid gets stranded in a Martian art gallery haunted by affectionate ghost dogs, and the artworks themselves are the puzzles.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are a family-friendly 1990s sci-fi platformer about a kid genius with a rocket, and a cute short horror about an art gallery haunted by licking ghost dogs. The decoded tags favoured Retro, Horror, Point & Click and Puzzle over Platformer, so I made it a cute-spooky point-and-click on Mars. Versions without the dogs scored worse.

ideas.title: The Last Löyly
ideas.short_description: A surreal first-person shooter in a sauna at the end of the world. Keep the stove burning, throw steam at the cold, and shoot back the frost that crawls out of the endless night.
ideas.description:
The Last Löyly is a surreal, psychedelic first-person VR shooter set in a Finnish sauna at the end of the world. One morning the sun did not rise. The lake froze to the bottom, the forest turned to glass, and the sauna on the shore became the only warm place left.

Between attacks you run the sauna as a realistic physics simulation. Split logs, feed the stove, carry water from the ice hole and keep the stones hot. Every ladle of water on the stones releases a wave of steam that heals you and pushes the cold back.

Then the frost comes to life. Ice figures, frozen elk and whispering shapes crawl over the snow toward the light. Hold them off with an old hunting shotgun, a flare pistol and buckets of boiling water, aiming by hand in VR or with a mouse on a flat screen.

Stay in the heat too long and the steam brings psychedelic visions of the summer that is gone. Survive the long night and find out why the sun went out.
ideas.pitch: A first-person survival shooter where the base you defend is a working sauna sim: heat the stones, throw steam to heal and push back the cold, and shoot living frost at the end of the world, with psychedelic steam visions.
ideas.interpretation: This hole sits right beside Saunageddon, a sauna investigation comedy, inside a ring of first-person VR, realistic-sim, psychedelic and shooter games. The decoded tags are First-Person, Action, Simulation, Shooter, Atmospheric, VR and Realistic. So the gap is a sauna game that is an atmospheric VR shooter and simulation rather than a dialogue-led investigation.

ideas.title: Spellbook Mixtape
ideas.short_description: A nostalgic 2D deckbuilding adventure set in a wizard academy whose worlds look like strange 1990s music videos. Build a spellbook of cards, duel odd creatures and unravel why the music professor vanished.
ideas.description:
The music professor of a floating wizard academy has gone rogue, and the songs that hold its worlds together are falling silent. As a first-year student with a battered spellbook, you set out through twenty strange worlds that look like forgotten 1990s music videos: neon highways full of space cars, chrome deserts guarded by grinning demons, and cities of giant talking heads.

Explore each world in colourful 2D pixel art, chat with its odd residents and collect clues about the professor's disappearance. When trouble starts, combat switches to turn-based card duels. Your spells are cards drawn from a deck you build yourself: fire, frost, thunder, bloom and dream schools, each with its own sound. Play cards that share a key and they layer into a song that grows more powerful each turn.

Between worlds you return to the academy to craft new spell cards, swap tracks with classmates and decorate your dorm. Light puzzles, a gentle difficulty curve and a mystery told across every world make it a cozy, nostalgic deckbuilding adventure for anyone who grew up with wizard school stories.
ideas.pitch: A wizard-school deckbuilder where every spell is a musical phrase and every world is a surreal retro-futuristic 1990s music video, so building your deck also means composing the soundtrack.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are a whimsical wizard deckbuilding MMORPG and a psychedelic retro-futuristic VR music ride. The decoded tags (2D, Pixel Graphics, 1990's, Deckbuilding, Mystery) pointed to a nostalgic 2D card adventure, so I fused them as spells-as-songs inside music-video worlds. VR-ride readings scored much lower.

ideas.title: Starfall Over Taihoku
ideas.short_description: During the air raids of 1945 Taipei, a schoolgirl finds a crashed rocket that is not from this world. An anime sci-fi action RPG that begins in wartime and ends in space.
ideas.description: In the last summer of the war, sirens sound over Taipei almost every day. Lin Mei-hua is fourteen, and she has learned to run when the sirens start. One morning, in a crater by the river, she finds a sleek silver rocket that no army built, and a small voice inside it asking for help. Starfall Over Taihoku is a 2D anime action-adventure in two halves. On the ground, you sneak through bombed streets and shelters, gathering parts and keeping the rocket secret while helping neighbors survive the raids. Then the rocket wakes, and the story leaves the earth: pilot it in fast side-scrolling shooter stages through orbit, asteroid belts and the derelict stations of the travelers who lost it. Salvage you bring back levels up the rocket's weapons and shields, while the friends Mei-hua makes along the way unlock new skills and story paths. Every chapter is told through hand-drawn scenes and quiet conversations about family, loss and courage. The goal is to send the stranger home before the war ends, and to decide what Mei-hua will carry back down to earth.
ideas.pitch: An anime story-driven action RPG that joins a historical home-front survival story (1945 Taipei under air raids) to a space shooter, as a schoolgirl repairs and flies home an alien rocket she found in a bomb crater.
ideas.interpretation: The hole sits between an anime/JRPG/space-shooter cluster and a WWII-Taiwan adventure parent (Raid on Taihoku), with rocket and asteroid parents. Its decoded tags are Action, Adventure, Anime, Sci-fi, Space, RPG, Shooter and Story Rich. Combining the wartime-Taipei and alien-rocket parts got much closer than a pure anime space RPG did.

ideas.title: Bearer of the Lamp
ideas.short_description: Step inside a faithful VR reconstruction of Queen Nefertari's tomb in this asymmetric multiplayer thriller. The lamp bearer reads the painted walls to reach the burial chamber; the agile ba-bird flock hunts the bearer through the dark to seize the light and take their place.
ideas.description:
The tomb of Nefertari, great royal wife of Ramesses II, has been rebuilt in virtual reality, chamber by chamber, with its painted gods and spells restored to their original colours. Every match takes place inside it.

The Bearer plays in VR with the only lamp. Step inside at true scale, raise the light to reveal murals and hieroglyphs, and handle interactive reconstructions that explain the history, building methods and mythology behind each scene. Every scene understood opens a sealed door. When the flock attacks, focus the lamp into a beam to fend off the monsters and survive.

The Flock plays on desktop as ba-birds, the human-headed souls of ancient Egyptian belief. Agile and fast in the dark, they swoop through shafts and side passages, but the light burns them. Hunt down the Bearer from the shadows, and whoever lands the final blow takes the lamp and becomes the new Bearer.

Play solo against an AI flock, or online with friends. Between matches, an in-game museum gathers everything you have discovered.
ideas.pitch: An educational VR tomb reconstruction turned into the arena of an asymmetric hunt: the VR player has to study the real paintings to progress while desktop players, as ba-bird souls, try to steal the lamp.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are Nefertari: Journey to Eternity (an educational VR tour of a historical tomb) and The Flock (an asymmetric thriller where agile monsters hunt whoever carries a light artifact and take their place). The decoded tags are 3D, Simulation, Exploration, VR, Historical and Action, so the tomb tour became the match arena and the flock became Egyptian ba-birds. A single-player survival version scored lower than the asymmetric one.

ideas.title: The Last Updraft
ideas.short_description: Two estranged sisters, one last glider race across the ruined valley they grew up in. Play the story alone against your rival sibling, or split the screen with a friend and fight over every shortcut, memory and finish line in versus mode.
ideas.description:
Years after the war emptied the valley, the old glider race returns for one final season. Ada and June used to fly it together. Now they barely speak, and both of them have entered.

Every chapter is a head-to-head race between the sisters, part sport, part argument. You launch from broken towers, ride the wind through collapsed bridges and overgrown factories, and fight for the faster line. Between races, each sister explores the valley on foot, finds old letters and photographs, and solves small puzzles that open new routes: a shortcut their father built, a thermal above the dam where they once crashed.

In single-player you choose a sister and race the other, whose flying changes with what you learn about her. In versus mode, two players take a sister each in split-screen or online, and the story's ending depends on who wins the final course. A competitive sports game about family, rivalry and finally saying sorry.
ideas.pitch: A story-driven PvP sports game: the whole narrative is a head-to-head glider rivalry between two sisters, and when two players take a sister each, whoever wins the versus final decides how the story ends.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags (Action, Adventure, Puzzle, PvP, Racing, Sports, Post-apocalyptic) and the memory-driven parents and neighbours (ToMyX, The Squirrel & Sea, A Glider's Journey, When We Disappear) point to an emotional story told through a competitive sport. Score rose most when PvP versus play became the core of the story, not a side mode.

ideas.title: Spike of Peace
ideas.short_description: No more battles. The elves and dwarves will settle their war with volleyball. Dive, spike and survive spell-filled rallies as a young elf who never wanted to fight.
ideas.description:
Spike of Peace is a colourful third-person physics volleyball game, cute on the surface, difficult in the hands and emotional at heart. For a hundred years elves and dwarves fought over the valley; now every border is decided by a match on the sand.

You play as Lirra, a young elf who lost her brother in the last battle and now captains a village team nobody believes in. The campaign is an action roguelike road trip: each run brings random rivals, courts and blessings that change how the ball flies. Lose a match and the road starts again, but your friends grow closer every time.

Rallies are physics-driven and difficult. You control every jump, dive and spike, and dwarf teams hurl enchanted serves that burst into storms of bouncing orbs, so each point becomes a small bullet hell you survive with timing and nerve.

Between matches, quiet story scenes deal with friendship, old grudges and what peace really costs. Play solo, or bring a friend for split-screen two-on-two.
ideas.pitch: A fantasy war replaced by a volleyball tournament: hard, physics-driven 3D rallies where enemy spells turn each point into a small bullet hell, built as an emotional action-roguelike road trip with split-screen 2v2.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags point to cute, colourful, difficult 3D third-person physics action with roguelike, bullet-hell, sports and emotional elements, plus split-screen modes. Single-tag probes favoured Elves, Volleyball, War and Emotional, and pushed away from mystery and detective themes. So the game is a heartfelt fantasy-war story played out as volleyball.

ideas.title: Bert's Big Week
ideas.short_description: The new mayor of a tiny mountain village has one week before the zombies arrive. Solve silly point-and-click puzzles by day, then click your way through the night defending the town you just about held together.
ideas.description: Bert's Big Week is a comedic pixel art adventure with a tower defense twist. Bert won the election in a village of forty people because nobody else ran, and on his first day the radio announces a zombie outbreak heading up the valley. Days play like a classic point-and-click adventure: explore the village, talk to its odd residents, collect strange items and combine them to solve puzzles, from convincing the baker to make cement bread to teaching the goat to guard the gate. Every solved problem becomes something useful for the night: a pie catapult, a scarecrow trap, a volunteer with a frying pan. When the sun sets, the view switches to a top-down map of the village. Place your defenses along the lanes, click on shuffling zombies to bonk them, and spend the coins they drop on quick upgrades while the waves grow sillier and bigger. Survive the week, keep everyone in one piece and uncover where the zombies came from.
ideas.pitch: A classic comedy point-and-click adventure where every puzzle you solve by day becomes a defence for that night's clicker tower-defence siege by goofy zombies.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags are pixel-art 2D point & click comedy adventure (Nelson and the Magic Cauldron, Death Corp) mixed with Strategy, Zombies and Top-Down (Lord Clicker, Before the Snow, Pixel Combat). A day/night split covers both: adventure puzzles by day, clicker tower defence by night. A potion-brewing version and a pure clicker version scored lower.

ideas.title: Home Field '98
ideas.short_description: Summer, 1998. June's backyard is the only field on the block, so every kid in the neighbourhood plays football at her house. They don't know it is haunted. Win cute retro football games by day, and face a point-and-click psychological horror by night.
ideas.description:
Home Field looks like the 1990s sports games you played as a kid: chunky top-down pixel art, cheerful music and simple controls that let anyone pick up and play football. Choose your team from the kids on your street, each with a nickname, a favourite play and a secret, and score touchdowns between the swing set and the garden shed. A friend can take the rival team in local versus play.

But June lives in the house beside the field, and it is not empty. As the summer goes on, the matches change. Players vanish from the roster, the crowd stops cheering and the windows watch every down.

When the others go home, explore the house in point-and-click scenes. Talk to parents who will not answer, search the attic and basement, and help June balance a normal childhood with the horrors waiting upstairs.

Winning and losing both move the story forward. A perfect season opens some doors; a bad loss opens others. Play through a summer of friendship, rivalry and dread, and decide which memories are worth keeping.
ideas.pitch: A cute 1990s kids' football game where the field is the backyard of the heroine's haunted house: the matches and the point-and-click horror affect each other, and wins and losses both move the story forward.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are Backyard Football '99 (cute, simple-control kids' football) and GESTALT: The Fifth Day (a girl living in a haunted house, point-and-click psychological horror where success and failure both progress the story). The decoded tags are led by 1990's, 2D, Psychological Horror and Retro, with a local PvP signal. So the backyard football field belongs to the haunted house itself. A cursed-cartridge version and a horror-first version scored lower.

ideas.title: Mallet Marshal
ideas.short_description: Command a tiny army with nothing but a mallet. Tap to march, knock twice to charge, and whack the moles and goblins that pop out of the battlefield, one clumsy swing at a time.
ideas.description:
Mallet Marshal is a casual VR physics strategy game. A tiny army lives in a field full of holes, and you are the giant with the mallet.

Your soldiers are brave but not very bright. Tap one and it marches where it faces, knock it twice and it charges, knock the ground and the whole squad digs in. Enemy troops march in from the far side, while moles, beetles and burrowing goblins pop up from the holes in between, and every one of them can be whacked too.

The trick is choosing what to hit. Each swing either commands a unit or fights an enemy, never both, so every second is a quick tactical decision. Physics does the rest: soldiers tumble, shields bounce, and a wild swing can send your own captain flying.

Minimalist toy-box visuals, short rounds, a score attack ladder and a two-handed hard mode keep the mallet busy.
ideas.pitch: A real-time tactics game in VR where your only input is a clumsy mallet: every swing either gives an order to your tiny soldiers or whacks an enemy popping out of the holes, never both.
ideas.interpretation: The hole sits among VR whack-a-mole, minimalist placement-strategy, physics-building and VR tower-defense games. The decoded tags are casual, strategy, simulation, physics, VR, minimalist, tactical and comedy, and probes rewarded Intentionally Awkward Controls and Real Time Tactics. So the gap is a strategy game whose command system is a whack-a-mole mallet.

ideas.title: Ashgrove After Dark
ideas.short_description: Run a small shelter for strange creatures at the edge of an empty town that rearranges itself every night. Explore its streets in first person, take in what you find, and send your creatures into turn-based battles against the things that follow you back.
ideas.description:
The shelter on Ashgrove Lane was cheap for a reason. The town beyond the gate has been empty for years, and every night its streets, shops and apartments quietly swap places. The creatures that wander out of it are not in any book.

By day you run the shelter: cook feed, build pens, clean, heal and befriend residents like the lantern-cat, the paper fox and the slow, enormous moss-hound. By dusk you walk into town with a flashlight, mapping streets that will be gone tomorrow, solving small puzzles to open locked buildings, and searching for new creatures. Other keepers can join your town online to explore with you, or face your creatures in turn-based PvP duels.

Some things in the town do not want to be found. When they catch up with you, your creatures fight in turn-based battles where trust, mood and the light you carry matter as much as strength. A cozy management sim slowly turning into something stranger.
ideas.pitch: A cozy creature-shelter management sim joined to first-person exploration of a town that rebuilds itself every night, where the creatures you care for fight in turn-based battles that depend on their trust and mood, against the town's horrors or against other keepers online.
ideas.interpretation: The parents mix creature care (Dragon Shelter, Familiars.io), a creeping board-game corruption (The Encroaching) and apartment horror (Dead Stop - The Tenant), and the decoded tags are Exploration, Simulation, Casual, Strategy, PvP, Turn-Based Combat and Psychological Horror. I read this as a cozy creature sim that slowly turns into horror. An urban setting scored better than a forest one, and so did a PvP mention placed early in the text.

ideas.title: Night Choir
ideas.short_description: Ride a motorbike through the dreams of a sleeping town. Race along roads built by music, fight off the riders of its nightmares, and piece together the story of the night everyone stopped waking up.
ideas.description: Night Choir is a third-person racing adventure set inside dreams. One night every resident of a small coastal town fell asleep and never woke. You arrive on an old motorbike and discover you can ride into their dreams, where roads are built from the music each sleeper remembers. Race along winding melodies over oceans, through ruined cathedrals and across endless rooftops, keeping your speed in time with the song to stop the road from collapsing. In the darker dreams, shadow riders hunt you down, and you fight back at full speed, shoving them off the road and breaking their chains before they reach the dreamer. Off the bike, explore each dream on foot, talk to the dreamers and find the memories that explain why they cannot wake. Each rescued sleeper adds a new instrument to your bike's radio and opens new roads. The whole journey can be played on a flat screen or in VR, and a split-screen mode lets two friends race the finished dream roads head to head. Atmospheric, musical and story-rich, it is a racing game you play for the journey.
ideas.pitch: A story-driven racing adventure where the tracks are built from music inside sleepers' dreams. You keep in time with the song so the road holds, fight nightmare riders at speed, and explore on foot to wake the town.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags read as a story-rich, atmospheric 3D third-person adventure with an odd Racing signal and some split-screen PvP. Its parents mix a musical VR relaxation space (SZEN), a brutal fantasy sport and medieval RPGs. Medieval racing versions scored ~0.23; adding SZEN's music and dreamlike side to a racing adventure, with combat and split-screen, scored best. I left out the adult tags that the void's decoder also reads.

ideas.title: Wren and Clover
ideas.short_description: A young noble girl and her little tank must prepare their tiny country for war. Recruit knights, archers and cooks, and get everyone ready in time.
ideas.description: Her name is Wren. Her tank is called Clover. Clover has never fired a shot; her grandfather swapped the cannon for a watering can. Roll across flower meadows, snowy passes and sandy beaches. Repair bridges, clear roads and rebuild windmills. Visit castles, farms and fishing villages, recruit knights, archers and cooks, and practise archery and horse riding with the old general. Every friend you make joins the cause with a skill of their own, and every upgrade makes Clover faster, stronger and a little bit cuter. Explore a big open countryside at your own speed and enjoy the beautiful scenery. No stress, no timers, just fun. Supports VR headsets and gamepads, and can also be played on a flat screen with a mouse and keyboard. When summer ends, all your preparation, and all the friends you made on both sides of the border, decide whether the war happens at all.
ideas.pitch: A cozy, no-combat 3D adventure RPG, playable in VR, where a noble girl and her repurposed tank get a tiny kingdom ready for a war through exploring, repairing and making friends, and may stop it from happening at all.
ideas.interpretation: Very casual, cute and relaxing fantasy with a female lead and VR, mixed with military and vehicle signals from the parents (the noble girl on the brink of war in Paths Taken, the Mars rover exploring and upgrading, a military strategy game). The top single-tag probes were Tanks, Military and Tabletop, and the anti-horror direction was strong, so I read it as a wholesome war-preparation road trip with a harmless tank.

ideas.title: Nightrotor
ideas.short_description: A retro 1990s action-adventure: pilot a deadly helicopter gunship into the darkness over a haunted island, battle the evil that waits below and complete dangerous night missions, where getting in is easy and getting out is hell.
ideas.description:
Inspired by the gunship flight games and survival horror classics of the 1990s, this new adventure puts our hero in the pilot's seat. Winter, 1996: command has lost contact with its island radar station. The island is pitch dark, the radio hisses with voices that should not be there, and the old mansion on its cliffs has every light burning.

Take off from a lonely carrier, fly low along cliffs and coves, and battle possessed soldiers, crawling things and flying shapes with your cannon, rockets and searchlight. Rescue survivors, escort supply boats and destroy the stone totems that keep the darkness alive.

Some objectives cannot be reached from the cockpit. Set down in a courtyard or on a rooftop and the game shifts to tense on-foot exploration of the mansion, where each room you clear reveals a new landing zone or a new piece of the mystery. Fuel, ammunition and armour are always scarce, so every sortie is a gamble. Chunky polygon graphics, arcade-friendly flight handling and a droning synth score complete the retro action horror experience.
ideas.pitch: A 1990s-style gunship action game whose mission map is a haunted-house survival horror: the island is fought from the air, the mansion is cleared on foot, and each one opens the way into the other.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are a retro 1990s helicopter gunship sim and a classic 1920s haunted-mansion survival horror. The decoded tags lean Action and Adventure first, with horror and retro as flavour, so the fusion is an action-first gunship campaign over a haunted island. Mansion landings advance the mystery rather than sitting apart as a separate mode.

ideas.title: Lena and the Endless Line
ideas.short_description: A collection of dozens of subway-flavoured microgames! Lena fell asleep on the U7 and now the ride never ends. Travel famous lines from Berlin to New York in a dream where every station is a quick, strange challenge and every passenger is one of the oddest characters you will ever meet.
ideas.description:
Every evening Lena takes the U7 home through Berlin. Tonight she dozed off between stations, and when the doors opened the platform was made of jelly, the conductor was a heron and the network map had grown lines to cities all over the world.

Ride one famous route after another, from Berlin and Paris to New York and Tokyo, each recreated in bright anime-style 2D with its real station names and its own dream twist. At every stop the doors open onto a microgame lasting a few seconds: hold the handrail through a sudden curve, stamp a ticket for a ghost, help a tourist find the exit or catch a train before it melts.

Clear enough stops to reach the end of the line and unlock the next city. Between rides, explore the dream carriages, chat with the strange regulars and collect souvenirs from every station. Some of them know the way back to the waking world.

A cheerful, surreal journey for anyone who has ever fallen asleep on the train.
ideas.pitch: A cheerful microgame collection built on real, famous subway lines: every station stop is a surreal few-second microgame in a commuter's never-ending dream, not another subway-anomaly horror game.
ideas.interpretation: The parents are Dreams of Aether (a surreal microgame collection with a female lead trapped in an endless dream) and World of Subways 2 (a realistic Berlin U7 route). The decoded tags are Casual, 2D, Adventure, Anime and Colorful, with no horror. Nightmare-train framings collapsed into the crowded subway-horror cluster, so the best version is a light-hearted dream ride along real lines.

ideas.title: The Hill Remembers
ideas.short_description: A psychological horror platformer about a child's red ball rolling down the endless hill of a town emptied by a catastrophe. Bounce and steer through ash-grey streets, and find out who keeps carrying you back to the top.
ideas.description: The Hill Remembers is an atmospheric 3D physics platformer about a red rubber ball that cannot stop rolling. The town on the hill was emptied in a single night when the sky turned grey, and every street leads down. Steer through yards, staircases, playgrounds and flooded basements, bounce off cars and fences, and use slopes and ramps to clear gaps and reach hidden paths. It begins almost cozy, the sun low and the streets quiet, but each time you reach the bottom, something carries you back to the top, and the town has changed. Doors are open that were closed. Toys have moved. A shape stands in the window of the house at the end of the road. The horror is psychological and slow, built from repetition, silence and small wrong details in a stylized, soft world. Runs are short and linear, controls are just steering and a bounce, and the story is told entirely through what you roll past.
ideas.pitch: A cozy roll-down-the-hill physics toy that turns into a looping psychological horror story: each time you roll down, the post-apocalyptic town at the bottom has changed in small, wrong ways.
ideas.interpretation: This hole sits between the cozy physics toy 'Roll it down the hill!', horror and post-apocalyptic cinematic platformers (Becloudead, SCP: Submerged, All Hallows) and a narrative object-platformer (DRIFTED). A rolling object in an emptied, slowly changing town covers all of them; a drifting-bag version came too close to DRIFTED.

ideas.title: Keeper of the Snowbound Keep
ideas.short_description: The siege is over and the snow is still falling. Clean up the aftermath, gather scattered arrows and lost belongings, patch the walls and get the castle ready for the next attack, alone or with friends.
ideas.description:
High in the mountains stands a realistic medieval castle, cut off by snow. All winter it held out against a siege, and now the enemy has gone, leaving broken carts, scattered arrows and frozen mud behind. Your grandfather was the castle's caretaker before you. Now the job is yours.

Work in first person through the realistic, snowbound keep. Shovel snow off the battlements, pull arrows from the gates, rebuild the walls stone by stone, and rescue the frightened horses, goats and chickens still hiding in the barn. Search the drifts for the belongings the villagers lost while sheltering inside, and sort the potions and spellbooks the old wizard left scattered across his study.

Then plan your season. Decide which repairs come first, where to store firewood and how to stock the cellar before the spring thaw opens the pass again, and whoever is waiting on the other side.

Play alone at a calm pace or bring up to three friends in online co-op to split the work. No combat and no blood, just the quiet satisfaction of turning a battered castle back into a home.
ideas.pitch: A nonviolent, realistic first-person co-op game set after a medieval siege: you don't fight the war, you clean up after it, searching for lost belongings, rescuing animals and rebuilding a snowbound castle.
ideas.interpretation: The decoded tags (Casual, Simulation, First-Person, Realistic, Co-op, Hidden Object, Family Friendly) and parents (wizard-tower organizing, a grave-relocation homecoming walk) point to a calm, realistic hands-on sim. Probing the direction showed it pushes hard away from space and sci-fi and toward medieval, snow, organizing and siege themes, so I read it as a cozy aftermath and cleanup sim in a castle.
